text:
To all the jobseekers-

I know the market is tough.
I also had a difficult time looking for a new role.

Just don't give up.
Not everything is your fault.

You can just try your best.
Give it all in.

Be brave.
Face the hardship.
Hold on for a while.

I know the time is rough but in the end it'll be all worth it.

You are enough.
Don't stop doubting your skills and preparation.

Time is tough and so are you.

I have met a lot of people in corporate till now. 

And more than talking, I’ve always preferred observing.

One pattern I’ve quietly noticed:
The ones who micro-manage,
who track every minute,
who treat you less like a human and more like a machine…
…are often fighting battles you don’t see.

Not with you.
With themselves.

Because when someone is truly secure,
they don’t need to control every move you make.

When there’s a void in personal life,
when there’s a lack of control somewhere else,
it slowly finds its way into the workplace.

And control becomes their coping mechanism.
Dominance becomes their comfort zone.
Not because they’re strong -
but because something inside feels weak.

This isn’t a justification.
But it is an understanding.

Because once you see this,
you stop taking things personally.
You stop reacting.
You start observing.

Fragile egos don’t need confrontation.
They need distance, boundaries, and quiet confidence.

And that’s how you win in corporate -
not by overpowering others,
but by not letting their chaos overpower you.

The Age gap in Corporate is so weird and wild.

My corporate mortal enemy is around 50 years old
and
My corporate bestie is around 65 years old.

Corporate taught me one thing:

Age doesn’t define maturity.

One will ruin your day in a meeting,
the other will save your career in silence.

Same office. Same building.
Different species.

LinkedIn has become that one overachieving relative at every family function.

'Sharma ji ka beta got a job of 19084692369 INR what are YOU doing?'

Every post is either:

'My 48 start-ups failed but I never gave up'

or 

'I made 3 crores at 21, here's how can you too'

No one posts:

'I am confused'
'I don't know what I am doing'
'I cried yesterday for no reason'
'I applied to 180 jobs and got ghosted by all'

Because that thing - won't get you likes, won't get you comments.

So, we pretend, we all become - thought leaders, humbled learners, hustlers, philosphers..

LinkedIn is the only place where you are either building a start-up or building a personal brand or building anxiety. There is no 4th option.

Here is what i want you to know -

Most people are still figuring it out.
Most people are lost.
Most people are just trying to get through the day without feeling like a failure.

And that is raw, that is okay.

Till then, please read how waking up at 5 am changed my life stories on LinkedIn, it is okay if you are going to read it at 2 am, questioning your existence - because that my friend is also a part of life :)

Your LinkedIn feed is lying to you.
Not because people are fake.

But because nobody posts the middle.

You’ll see:

Offer letter
Promotion
New role

But you’ll never see:

The 47 rejections
The silent breakdowns
The 'am I even good enough?' phase

Success looks loud online.
But in reality,
it’s built in very quiet, very uncomfortable phases
no one claps for.

If you’re in that phase right now,
you’re not behind.
You’re just not posting it.

Another uncomfortable thought:
If work is your entire personality, then you’re not living - you’re being utilised.
Some people don’t experience time.

They consume it in slots.
Even rest is 'well-deserved'.
Even joy needs justification.

They don’t sit with thoughts.
They schedule them.

The tragedy isn’t working hard.
The tragedy is outsourcing meaning to a payslip.

Philosophers warned us about this long ago -
when identity collapses into function, humans become tools that applaud their own usefulness.

Titles feel permanent until they aren’t.
Calendars feel important until they stop filling themselves.

And when work finally goes quiet - layoffs, burnout, weekends, retirement -
there’s a strange silence no KPI prepares you for.

Because if you only know how to be productive,
you don’t know how to be present.

Work should sharpen you.
Not replace you.

A life that cannot slow down
is not ambitious -
it’s afraid of stillness.

Job hunting in India is not for the weak.

You’ll see a post that says 'We’re urgently hiring!'
You apply in 30 seconds.
And they ghost you faster than your ex.

'Easy Apply' feels like Tinder.
You swipe, they ignore.
And somewhere, HR writes - 'We’ll get back to you.'

You update your resume 47 times, change fonts, remove hobbies, add buzzwords like 'team player', 'growth mindset', and 'Excel wizard'…
Still no reply.
Meanwhile on LinkedIn:
People with 2 connections and 0 experience write -
'I’m thrilled to announce I’ve joined Google.'
And you’re sitting there thinking -
Maybe I should be 'thrilled' to announce that I’m still unemployed.

But here’s the truth:
You’re not lazy.
You’re not behind.
You’re just living in a country where 'experience required: 3 years' comes in intern listings.
So hang in there.

Because one day, you’ll get that offer.
And your 'We’re happy to have you onboard' email will feel like a national award.
I once wrote a PRD so detailed it could’ve replaced me. Now I just write bullet points, because I’ve accepted my fate - no one reads them anyway.

Nobody talks about this phase in corporate.

You’re not failing.
But you’re not growing either.

You’re just… existing.

Doing tasks.
Attending meetings.
Replying 'Noted'.

Days pass.
Weeks pass.
Nothing changes.

And the scary part?
You get used to it.

Comfort is dangerous like that.
It doesn’t hurt.
But it slowly kills ambition.

So if you feel stuck,
that discomfort you’re avoiding
might actually be your way out.

Your manager is not your mentor.

Sometimes they are.
Most times, they’re just managing deliverables.

They care about deadlines.
Not your dreams.

And that’s okay.

Because expecting growth from someone
who is measured on output
is setting yourself up for disappointment.

Find mentors outside reporting lines.
Build your own learning system.

Because careers don’t grow in performance reviews.
They grow in what you do after work.

There are two types of people in meetings.

One who speak a lot
and say very little.

And one who speak less
but change the direction of the room.

Corporate rewards visibility.
But impact doesn’t always come from noise.

Sometimes,
the most powerful thing you can say is
just one clear sentence.

So don’t confuse volume with value.

You don’t hate your job.
You hate what it’s doing to your life.

The long hours.
The constant pressure.
The Sunday anxiety.

Work was supposed to support life.
Not consume it.

But somewhere along the way,
we normalized burnout
and called it ambition.

Maybe success isn’t about doing more.
Maybe it’s about needing less from work
to feel okay.

Early in your career,
you think hard work is enough.

Then you realize:

Visibility matters.
Communication matters.
Positioning matters.

You can be the smartest person in the room
and still be overlooked.

Not because you’re not capable.
But because no one knows.

Corporate is not just about doing the work.
It’s about making sure the work is seen.
